Pluralism

/PLOOR-uh-liz-um/ - the stress falls on PLOOR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Pluralism means the coexistence and acceptance of many different groups, beliefs, or traditions.

The choir director ran the season on cheerful pluralism, letting gospel, plainchant, and pop share one program without ranking them.

Worked Example

When the new nation wrote its constitution, the drafters faced three living systems of law — civil courts in the cities, religious courts in the north, and village councils everywhere else. Rather than crown one, the charter recognized all three, each supreme in its own sphere, with a mixed bench to referee the borders between them. Foreign observers called the design pluralism in its purest form.

Pluralism goes beyond tolerance: tolerance puts up with difference, while pluralism means the coexistence and acceptance of many groups, beliefs, or traditions — difference designed in, not merely endured. It names a standing arrangement, which is why constitutions and charters are where the word does its work.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

multiculturalism: many cultures specifically, rather than beliefs or traditions generally

inclusiveness: the habit of welcoming everyone in, without a system behind it

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

monoculture: a single culture crowding out all others

conformity: everyone bending to one accepted way

Where it sits · how deeply difference is woven in — tolerance → acceptance → pluralism

tolerance vs. pluralism: Tolerance puts up with difference and stops there, well short of pluralism.

acceptance vs. pluralism: Acceptance goes further than tolerance, welcoming difference rather than enduring it, but pluralism goes further still: it builds the whole arrangement around many groups living side by side.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — plural

Root — plural: more than one (Latin pluralis, from plus, more)

Suffix — -ism

Suffix — -ism: system or principle of

Put it together

Put it together: Plural (more than one) + -ism (a system or principle) = the principle of more-than-one. Grammar borrowed plural for nouns beyond the singular; political philosophy took the next step, making an -ism of the conviction that a society can hold more than one faith, culture, or tradition without having to choose among them.

Use the root in a new word: plurality

Use the root in a new word: plurality: With four candidates splitting the vote, she won on a plurality of 38 percent.

Word Choice

formal / civic

Pluralism is the word of charters, courts, and civics classes — it names a standing arrangement, not a mood. Its neighbor in this unit is cosmopolitan: a cosmopolitan person or city is at ease among many cultures, while pluralism is the principle that lets those cultures keep their own shape side by side. For the simple fact of mixture, variety is enough.
